newsitem.title: USA: Are high-yield bond funds junk?.
newsitem.headline: Are high-yield bond funds junk?.

text.p: Does anyone remember what happened to high-yield bond funds during the last recession?

These days, high-yield bond funds (also known as junk bond funds) are the toast of the fixed-income side of town. The reason: High-yield bond funds have gained 16 percent annually since 1991, versus only 7.2 percent for high-quality corporate bond funds. Junk funds have done almost as well as stock funds, which have gained 17.2 percent during the same period.

Before you jump into junk, however, think back to 1990 when many junk bond fund investors suffered losses of 18 percent or more. Often, those investors bought shares in junk funds with the understanding that their money would be safe -- after all, the funds held bonds, didn't they?

Trouble is, high-yield bonds also can carry a high degree of risk. The reason: They invest in bonds of companies that have credit ratings below investment grade. Such companies generally are in mediocre or even bad financial condition.

Most companies that issue high-yield bonds are perfectly capable of making timely interest and principal payments to the investors who hold their bonds -- as long as the economy is relatively strong. But a sharp economic downturn or an industry setback can raise questions about their ability to keep doing so. When that occurs, the bonds of some issuers--especially the most marginal ones -- are likely to plummet in price.

During the past five years, the economy has been strong. What's more, bond market fluctuations have been driven largely by interest rate moves, which typically have a greater impact on investment-grade bonds with relatively low yields. Thus, junk bonds have delivered higher returns -- and have been less volatile than supposedly safer high-quality bonds issued by government or blue chip companies.

No wonder junk funds are popular. But what happens when the economy stumbles and junk bonds take a beating? If history is any guide, shareholders in junk funds might rush to get out of the high-yield market. That would force funds to raise cash by disgorging their bond holdings, driving prices down even further.

Such a downturn could be a great buying opportunity -- but only for investors who understand the risks and are willing to stay with the high-yield sector for the long term. With that in mind, here are a few rules for investing in high-yield funds, and a few funds to consider for the long-term.

Rule One: Make sure the fund manager can tell a solid high-yield bond from a real piece of junk. Some investors have begun throwing money at anything that pays a high yield, and some fund managers are no better. But fund managers who are willing and able to do serious research often can find bargains among bonds of companies whose financial strength is underrated.
Their funds can provide extra yield and the potential for capital gains as other investors discover their bargains and bid up the bonds' prices.
Rule Two: Diversify. Choose a fund that holds a wide range of issues in different regions and economic sectors. A heavy concentration in one industry's junk bonds can be disastrous.

Rule Three: Plan to invest for at least five years and be sure you mean it. The next downturn in the high-yield market will likely be vicious. Be sure that you can truly tolerate a big loss in your high-yield holdings. If you can't, then mix them up with high-quality bond funds or go entirely with funds that shun the junk market.

Still interested in junk? The best funds out there include MainStay High-Yield Corporate Bond (800-522-4202; $500 minimum investment; 5 percent load). The fund has gained 14.4 percent during the past five years, versus 11.5 percent for the average high-yield bond fund. What's more, the fund's managers buy mostly bonds with relatively high credit quality for the junk sector, making the fund only about 40 percent as risky as its peers during the past five years.

Nicholas Income (800-227-5987; $500 minimum; no-load) holds only bonds rated B or better. That approach can cause the fund to lag its peers when the junk bond market is roaring, but it should help the fund hold up relatively well during the next recession.

More aggressive investors might consider Invesco High-Yield (800-525-8085; $1,000 minimum, no-load). Manager Jerry Paul, who took the fund's reins in 1994, mixes higher-quality junk bonds with lower-rated securities that have helped to boost the fund's returns during recent years.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
